## Chapter 29

The years hurried past and left no time to reckon gains or losses. Winters vanished; springs burst into flower; Paris opened its arms and shut them again; and at last Adams, driven by weather and weariness, crept back to a garret in the Avenue du Bois and hid there for long summers in ignorance and silence, letting life find its own drift. After so many efforts to discover his direction, the drift itself seized him and swept him, as though he were a weed, forward and back with a steady seaward set. He had exhausted auto-motion. Without knowing Faraday, he found himself mimicking Faraday’s way of seeing lines of force everywhere he had once seen lines of will; images arranged themselves like attractions; repulsions counted only as battles of attractions; and so, by the shortest path, the mind stumbled into the mechanical theory of the universe and began another phase of education.

This was the work of the dynamo and the Virgin of Chartres. Force—the sink of all science—had, for thousands of years, been felt as occult attraction—love of God and lust for power in a future life. After 1500, as the attraction waned, men fell back on a vis a tergo—some instinct of danger behind—like Darwin’s survival of the fittest; and Pascal, great mind between Descartes and Newton, saw the master-motor in ennui: “I have often said that all the troubles of man come from his not knowing how to sit still.” Restlessness alone drove action. “So passes the whole of life. We combat obstacles in order to get repose, and, when got, the repose is insupportable; … ennui would of its own accord spring up from the depths of the heart … and would fill the mind with its venom.”

“If goodness lead him not, yet weariness
May toss him to My breast.”

Ennui, like Natural Selection, might account for change; it gave no direction. Direction required attraction, and attraction must be outside; some shaping influence. The schools had called it God. Caring little for names and fixed only on tracing Force, Adams went straight to the Virgin at Chartres and begged her to show him God as she did St. Bernard. She replied with the old kindness and a young mother’s pity for masculine dulness: You seek Christ through me? You are welcome; but he and I are one. We are Love. We meddle little with God’s other energies which are infinite and not knowable to man. If you are troubled by ignorance, look how I am ringed by masters; ask them!

Her honesty carried more conviction than science’s formula: the Virgin confessed her interest to be human, and sent him to Thomas Aquinas. Thomas, unlike modern physicists, answered plain: Christ and the Mother are one Force—Love—simple, single, sufficient for human wants; but Love acts so partially that philosophers can count on no share. Therefore turn to Christ and the Schools who represent all other Force. We deal with Multiplicity and call it God. After the Virgin redeems by her personal Force all that is redeemable in man, the Schools embrace the rest and give it Form, Unity, Motive.

The chart was easier than any other. One had but to do what the Church promised—blot out in a flash not only man but the Church, the earth, the planets, the sun—to clear the air without affecting mediæval science. Abolish the solar system and look at God as actual: continuous movement, universal cause, interchangeable energy. It was pantheism; but the Schools were pantheist enough; their deity the ultimate energy whose thought and act were one.

Rid of man, Thomas’s universe seemed almost more scientific than Haeckel’s or Mach’s. Contradiction for contradiction; attraction for attraction; energy for energy: Thomas linked together the joints of his machine while modern science offered neither proof nor scheme of reconciliation between thought and mechanics. The thirteenth century took mind for a mode of force directly derived from the intelligent prime motor; cause of form and sequence; therefore the only proof of unity. Without thought in the unit, no unity; without unity, no order; thought alone was Form; Mind and Unity flourished or perished together.

The lesson startled even a man long jaded with lessons. If he must insist on a Universe, he seemed driven to the Church. Science guaranteed no unity. The student felt, like his predecessors, meshed in religion’s drag-net. Men escaped the dilemma by ignoring it, or by seeing the Church reject pantheism as worse than atheism; but logic itself is the mind’s mirror and a dangerous trap, as Socrates taught. Generation after generation had gone down into these catacombs and stayed there, pursuing ignorance in company with the greatest names, none finding a highroad of escape. Adams cared little to escape; but he could not stop—even to gossip with Spinoza or St. Thomas—without either affirming unity or denying it. To deny would need a new education; at sixty-five, a meagre promise.

He had taken science’s word that the new unit was found; after sixty years he seemed to see its final synthesis in the kinetic theory of gases: space full of molecules flying in right lines at velocities up to a mile a second, colliding up to seventeen million times a second; matter reducible to such motion; perhaps the atom itself to pure motion. Then scientific “unity” turned out to be scientific analysis—Multiplicity. If one dropped the sounder into this abyss and frankly gave up Unity—what then? Science contented itself with a “larger synthesis,” which meant chaos for man. The anarchist bomb bade one go on. He dipped Descartes, Hume, Berkeley; wrestled Kant; pondered Hegel, Schopenhauer, Hartmann; strayed with Greeks—merely to ask what Unity meant and what happened when one denied it.

Apparently one never did. Every philosopher affirmed it, sane or not. Metaphysics turned contradiction into one Will or one representation. The universe could be known only as motion of mind, and therefore as unity; psychology was all. Of all pessimisms, the metaphysical was to a historian the least enticing. Introspection was the cruelest tragedy; nearly all high intelligence had drowned in it, while bovine survivors told the truth to no effect. The new psychology deepened the abyss: multiple personalities—telephonic centres and systems—dualism as common as binary stars; alternating selves even among friends; dreams that acted like strangers to the self; facts certain enough, asking only explanation.

The searcher of ignorance felt no call to causes, but saw the compound soul take the figure of a bicycle-rider who balanced himself by inhibiting inferior personalities, sure to fall into sub-conscious chaos if one of them got on top. The only absolute truth was the chaos below which any man could feel when he sought it. If mind was a magnet dispersing its lines of force in sleep and orienting them at waking, which was normal—dispersion or orientation? Sanity looked like an unstable artifice; one was an acrobat, with a dwarf on his back, crossing a chasm on a slack-rope, commonly breaking his neck. Ahead, no unity; behind, only thought as a continuous Force without race, sex, school, country, or church. History, to correct her errors in detail, must fix a scale for the whole, as space and time and force do. The mind needed a unit.

Eight or ten years led Adams to think he might take 1150–1250, expressed in Amiens and in Thomas Aquinas, as the point where man held his highest notion of himself as a unit in a unified universe; thence he could measure motion down to his own time without assuming truth beyond relation. He set himself to a study of thirteenth-century unity—Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres—and meant to label his own: The Education of Henry Adams: a Study of Twentieth-Century Multiplicity; from these two points to project lines forward and backward, subject to correction by any one who knew better. Thereupon he sailed for home.

## Chapter 30

Washington amused always; in 1900 as in 1800 its chief interest lay in distance from New York. New York’s movement had become planetary—beyond control—while Washington’s task, then as before, was to control it. For a student bred on Jefferson, Gallatin, Madison, Roosevelt’s attempt had vivid historic interest, but half a century must pass before forces could be measured; at least in foreign affairs one could see.

Hay stood at his summit and on the edge of wreck. He must keep China “open,” while China seemed about to be shut. Friendship reduced friction; good-will in London helped; and then, by a stroke, Germany swung. The Kaiser broke precedent, recalled his agent, and sent a personal representative to Washington. Whether he meant it or not, he gave the effect of meaning to assert independence of Russia. This refined policy raised the Kaiser’s ability in one’s scale and upset the centre of statesmanship. If Germany could be quickly detached and brought into an Atlantic system, a century of friction might be saved. Hay’s hands were freed to face Russia alone.

Russia was ten times harder. For two centuries Europe had done little but state the Russian problem. Adams’s family history made him grateful to the Czars and hopeful of the ultimate Atlantic combine that should allot the world among regulated activities; at the rate of unification since 1840, this might be possible within sixty years. Yet doubts and ignorance covered the field. Russian agents betrayed no depths; their philosophy, like their mass, was fatalism: Russia must roll; by irresistible inertia, she must crush whatever lay in her way. In 1903 one saw her knocking away the last blocks that held back the launch into the China Sea. The vast inertia called China would unite with the huge bulk of Russia, and the mass, once in motion, no new force could deflect.

The game seemed lost; the student cared chiefly for the game, not the stakes. He had equations to balance. The Atlantic had to deal with a continental ice-cap of vis inertiae. Was volume or intensity stronger? Where was the vis nova that could resist it? What was movement of inertia; what its law? Dictionaries said inertia was a property of matter by which it tended, at rest, to remain so, and, in motion, to move in a straight line. The mind, which knew itself neither at rest nor straight, substituted a mental analogue: the mind moved, when normal, about something it called a motive, and never without motives. So long as motives were habitual and their attraction regular, the movement might be called movement of inertia, to distinguish it from movement caused by newer or higher attractions; the greater the bulk to move, the greater the force needed to accelerate or deflect it.

Simple; and false by its simplicity. Minds were unequally inert. One class responded only to habit; another only to novelty. Race classified thought; class-lists classified mind; no two men thought alike; no woman thought like a man. Race-inertia seemed fairly constant, and made the chief trouble in the Russian future. History looked doubtful whether it had ever been overcome without destroying and reconstructing the race. Sex-inertia had never been overcome at all. Of all movements of inertia, maternity and reproduction were the most typical; woman’s property of moving in a constant line forever united history in its only unbroken sequence. If laws of inertia were to be found anywhere, they should be found there. Americans, ostentatiously ignoring sex, left their chief difficulty untouched.

Here Adams felt himself an eighteenth-century remainder. Early Institutions bored him; Early Women became a passion. Without movement of sex, history was pedantry. He talked of little else with women, trying devices to disclose the sub-conscious. Ask, at dinner, why the American woman was a failure, and the cleverest neighbor would answer without a breath: “Because the American man is a failure!” She meant it. Adams owed more to women than to all American men he ever heard of, and caught himself affirming their superiority. The half-dozen about his table were exceptions? Then the half-dozen men were exceptions too. The question stung; the cleverer the woman, the less she denied the failure; she was bitter. She had failed to hold the family; her children ran away like chickens with first feathers; the family was extinct; she had failed to create a new society or to rule the old; the Church fallen, the State deaf, she had the theatre or the street to decorate. She might glitter with historic diamonds, sparkle with wit as brilliant as the gems, in rooms as splendid as Rome’s; but no one, except her own sex, knew enough to be worth dazzling. She had her own way without restraint; she did not know what to do with it. Never had the world known a more devoted mother, and at forty her task was over. In Washington for a hundred years she had every advantage; she had created a medley where nine men out of ten refused her appeal to be civilized, and the tenth bored her.

The student was not preaching; he was measuring. Artificial energy to the value of twenty or five-and-twenty million steam horse-power had been created in America since 1840, and as much more economized; socially it had been turned over to the woman, she being the chief object of expenditure and the household the only great extravagance. What should be the result? It was evident and undisputed. She had been set free—volatilized like Clerk Maxwell’s perfect gas—brought to the point of explosion like steam. Sails, steamers, hotels, boulevards swarmed with her; behind, in city, town, farmhouse, myriads of new types—type-writers, telephone-girls, shop-clerks, factory-hands; even the schoolmistresses were inarticulate. All these had been created since 1840; all were to show their meaning before 1940. Whatever they were, they were not content, and were as hungry for illusions as in the fourth century; but hunger gave no hint of direction. Could movement of inertia, inherent in function, take new direction except along lines of inertia? The most vital of problems.

The typical American man had his hand on a lever and his eye on a curve; his life depended on an average speed that rushed toward a hundred miles an hour; he could not admit emotions, anxieties, sub-conscious distractions, any more than whiskey or drugs, without breaking his neck. He could not run his machine and a woman too; he must leave her to find her way. She imitated him. The result was often tragic, but tragedy was feminine history. Woman’s force had counted as inertia of rotation, her axis the cradle and the family. If her force were diverted from its axis, it must find a new field, and the family must pay. So far as she succeeded, she must become sexless like the bees, leaving the old energy of inertia to carry on the race.

The story was not new. Women had rebelled for thousands of years; had made a fortress of religion; had buried themselves in the cloister, in self-sacrifice, in good works—or bad. The twelfth century swarmed with their illusions of heaven and hell—ambition, intrigue, jealousy, magic; the American woman had no illusions, no ambitions, nothing to rebel against except maternity; yet the rebels increased by millions till they blocked rebellion. Socialisms that promised paradise for every male cut off avenues of escape opened by capitalism; the future reserved for machine-made collectivist females stared her in the face. From the male she could expect no help; his instinct of power was blind. The Church had known more about women than science ever would; perhaps the woman chiefly made the Church as protest against man; perhaps the man chiefly overthrew it because it was feminine. Overthrown, she had no refuge except what the man made for himself. She was free; sexless; she had discarded what the male disliked; she secretly regretted the discard and could not go back; she must, like the man, marry machinery. Already the American man sometimes wondered to find himself regarded as sexless; the American woman was oftener surprised to find herself regarded as sexual.

No honest historian can take sides with or against the forces he studies. Even the extinction of the race should be a fact among vital statistics. Society talked, goaded by the President; the surface current set one way while the silent undercurrent ran the other; but truth lay unconscious in the woman’s breast. An elderly inquirer could not compel a census of desires; could not ask every young woman how many children she wanted; could not require, by law, the bearing of one baby before thirty at the Treasury’s expense under penalty of solitary confinement for life. He could draw no conclusions except from the birth-rate; he could not frankly discuss the matter with the girls who would have gladly discussed it, for Faust was helpless in the tragedy of woman. Marguerite alone could decide.

Between race-inertia and sex-inertia, the Russian problem almost seemed simpler. Race-inertia and bulk might perhaps be partly overcome; sex-inertia could not, without extinguishing the race; yet an immense force doubling every few years was working to overcome it. Before this ocean of darkest ignorance society was already engulfed. Washington, with its simple farm standards, Southern and Western habits, easy ethics and history, lived in illusions as complete as any; even there society was uneasy enough without further fretting. One was almost glad to be a horseshoe crab in Quincy Bay and say that nothing changed; the woman would swim about the ocean of time, as she had swum in the past, with the gar-fish and the shark, unable to change.

Reading Karl Pearson's Grammar of Science and Poincaré's La Science et l'Hypothèse, Adams heard beneath their equations the whisper that order was a convenience and chaos the only honest assertion science could make of the supersensual; even Euclidian geometry, Poincaré allowed, was not true but merely convenient. Science had abandoned unity, and the child of 1900 would be born into a multiverse rather than a universe.
